papers.title: Weight Coding: Evolving Web-Scale Recommenders through Direct Weight Edits with LLM Agents
papers.authors: Junpeng Hou, Jiaxing Qu, Derek Cheng, Jaewon Yang, Abhinav Naikawadi, Karthik Subbian
papers.abstract: Web-scale recommender models evolve primarily through retraining or fine-tuning. We propose \emph{weight coding}, a methodology for model evolution through direct, executable weight edits. A large language model (LLM) agent inspects model structure and parameters, formulates hypotheses, and implements edits using evaluation feedback. The loop progresses from localized changes to targeted searches and composition, allowing edited components to adapt to one another. A cached engine enables rapid forward evaluation without backpropagation. On Pinterest's 147M-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, weight coding improves held-out recall@10 of production model by up to 15.0 percentage points (+24\% relative) with few edits in about 1/4 GPU hours of a full post-training finetune, while a common launch only improves around 1\%. After reinitializing the entire 13.6M-parameter interaction module randomly while retaining the surrounding trained model, searching 2,448 mixing and normalization parameters yields 9.8 points above production. Offline gains span the full funnel including dense retrieval, generative retrieval and ranking, with up to 1.37B learnable parameters and different edits for each architecture. Steering edits provide explicit control of model performance over segments like freshness and product. Weight coding requires no serving change and online A/B tests increase saves per user from the edited retrieval source by 8.4\% to 10.7\%, aligned with the target business objectives. Our results establish weight coding as a practical and useful tool for model development and and behavioral control in a real web-scale production system, with potential to extend to both pre-training and post-training stages across the funnel.
papers.summary: Web-scale recommenders usually have to retrain or fine-tune to change behavior, which is expensive and makes it hard to steer exposure for a specific kind of content. Pinterest has an LLM agent edit production weights directly and keep or discard each change with forward evaluation, without backpropagation. On the 147-million-parameter Image Search two-tower retriever, a few edits raised Recall@10 by up to 15 percentage points on evaluation data not used to invent the edits, using about a quarter of the GPU hours of a full post-training fine-tune. In online A/B tests, saves per user from the edited retrieval source rose 8.4% to 10.7%, and the same process can steer exposure toward freshness or products.

papers.title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
papers.authors: Adeep Hande, Shaghayegh Agah, Neeraj Sharma, Karina Halevy, Sardar Hamidian
papers.abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.
papers.summary: Recommenders often spend exposure on popular items, so long-tail and cold-start items with few interactions are hard to rank well. This work partitions items by interaction frequency, uses an LLM to generate synthetic interactions, and boosts each group's ranking quality and coverage while keeping the drop in overall NDCG@20 within a bound. The best augmentation for each group is not simply additive. On an industrial dataset with a SASRec backbone, group NDCG@20 more than doubled for extreme long-tail items and rose 60% for regular long-tail items; on MovieLens-32M the same two groups improved by 40% and 25%, without a large drop in the overall metric.

papers.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Tiwari Ankit Satyaprakash, Adamya Shyam, Vikas Kumar, Bharti Rana, Venkateswara Rao Kagita
papers.abstract: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
papers.summary: In sequential recommendation, not every interaction in a user history needs the same depth of reasoning, but a typical Transformer still spends the same number of layers on every position. The new method assigns a recursion depth to each interaction, shares a middle block with key-value reuse, and uses gated attention to regulate context. On Amazon Video Games, Industrial and Scientific reviews, and MovieLens 1M, it raises Recall@5, NDCG@5, and MRR@5 by 2.28%, 2.50%, and 2.0% on average over the strongest baseline. In a matched-architecture comparison, it also uses less computation and fewer parameters.

papers.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
papers.authors: Binhui Xie, Jinmin Li, Haomiao Tang, Guangting Wang, Song Jin, Jianwei Zhu, Fengyun Rao, Jing Lyu
papers.abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.
papers.summary: WeChat commerce has to read product images, catalogs, and livestreams together, and a general multimodal model often misses the business context. Tencent released a family of multimodal models trained for e-commerce, in five sizes from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model that activates 3B parameters at a time. Training first raises the share of e-commerce data inside a diverse multimodal mix, then uses distillation and reinforcement learning so the model can answer directly or think first. On a suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks, the largest model surpasses substantially larger open-source flagships, and every size also beats a similarly sized Qwen3.5 on general benchmarks. The family already powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat and serves billion-scale requests each day.

papers.title: Know You Before You Speak: User World Modeling for LLM Personalization in Multi-Turn Conversation
papers.authors: Jiani Luo, Xiaoyan Zhao, Yang Zhang, Shuyi Miao, Bingbing Xu, Stefan Konigorski, Tat-Seng Chua
papers.abstract:
Personalized dialogue requires more than recalling explicit user histories: systems also need to infer hidden user states that evolve through interaction and shape appropriate response strategies. Existing memory- and profile-based methods primarily reuse observable user information, offering limited support for modeling user-state dynamics or selecting actions based on how they shape future user states. We propose PUMA (Prospective User world Modeling for Action Selection), a framework grounded in the Free Energy Principle (FEP) that formulates personalization as decision-making under partial observability, centered on an explicit user world model that captures latent user states and their action-conditioned dynamics. At each turn, PUMA maintains a belief over the user's hidden state, refines the user world model for observation generation and action-conditioned state transition, and selects dialogue actions by minimizing expected free energy—balancing epistemic and pragmatic objectives under a unified criterion. This formulation shifts personalization from passive memory retrieval to model-based decision-making over user evolution. We instantiate PUMA on healthcare-oriented counseling and motivational interviewing benchmarks with latent state annotations for rigorous evaluation. 
Experiments show that PUMA improves long-horizon dialogue outcomes while maintaining strong response quality, and a cross-dataset study demonstrates more reliable user-state estimation and next-state prediction. 
Our code is available at: https://github.com/Annie1161/PUMA.
papers.summary: In multi-turn dialogue, recalling what a user has already said is often not enough; the system also has to infer hidden states that change through the conversation and shape the next reply. The new framework treats personalization as decision-making under partial observability: each turn it keeps a belief over the user's hidden state, updates a user world model, and chooses the next action by minimizing expected free energy, balancing exploration of the state with the dialogue goal. It is evaluated on healthcare counseling and motivational interviewing benchmarks that include latent-state annotations, and it improves long-horizon dialogue outcomes while keeping response quality strong, with more reliable user-state and next-state estimates in a cross-dataset study.

scenario: Today's personalization papers circle one question: how recommendation and dialogue systems can spend compute and data where they are actually needed, without retraining a whole model. Some edit the weights of a production retriever and replace fine-tuning with forward evaluation. Some split items into popular and long-tail groups and use a language model to add interactions that lift long-tail ranking. Some let a sequential model decide, interaction by interaction, how deep to compute. On the commerce side, multimodal models are further trained for catalogs, search, and livestreams. In dialogue, systems begin to infer a user's hidden state before choosing the next reply, rather than only replaying history.
